features.heading: What kinds of bots there are and what they do
features.lead: A bot is more than an auto-reply. Here’s what you can hand over to it right now — with examples from everyday businesses.

items.title: Bot administrator
items.text: Answers customer questions 24/7: prices, services, address, opening hours, availability. It only knows your data and never makes things up.
items.example: Beauty salon: at 23:40 a client asks about manicure prices and free slots — the bot replies instantly and offers a time.

items.title: Bookings and requests
items.text: Collects name, service, preferred time and contact details. You get a ready request in Telegram or a spreadsheet — without ten clarifying messages.
items.example: Car service: a customer writes the car model and what’s knocking — the mechanic gets a request with a phone number and photos.

items.title: Reminders and win-backs
items.text: Reminds clients about appointments to cut no-shows, and brings back those who asked about prices and disappeared.
items.example: Dental clinic: a day before the visit — a reminder with “Confirm” and “Reschedule” buttons.

items.title: Shop assistant
items.text: Picks products for a request, answers about sizes, delivery and payment, and sends links to the right items.
items.example: Clothing store: a shopper sends their height and measurements — the bot suggests a size and links the product.

items.title: Content on autopilot
items.text: Finds material, writes posts and publishes them on schedule, with automated checks before every post.
items.example: Real estate agency: every morning the channel gets a selection of new listings and market news.

items.title: Reports and notifications
items.text: Watches requests, the website and key numbers, and sends a summary or a notification when something goes wrong.
items.example: Café: every evening the owner gets a Telegram message with how many requests came in and from which channels.

cases.heading: My projects
cases.lead: Most of my commercial work is under NDA: IT is a small world, and clients don’t like being shown off. So here is what I built for myself — it shows how I think and what I can do.

items.title: My own AI chatbot engine for businesses
items.task: One codebase for bots of different businesses: answer customers in every messenger, never make things up and never waste the client’s money.
items.solution: The bot works in Telegram, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook Messenger and website chat and connects to any AI model. It handles common questions with ready answers without the AI, and the rest strictly from the business description. No answer, or the customer asks for a human — it calls the manager in Telegram.
items.result: A new business is connected without touching the code: its own folder with prices, answers and instructions. A daily per-person question limit protects against unnecessary AI bills.

items.title: Good-5 — an AI bot that runs a Telegram news channel by itself
items.task: Publish fresh news in Ukrainian and Russian every morning — with no manual work.
items.solution: The system collects about 100 news items a day from 15 sources, picks the 5 best and writes the texts from the originals — separately in each language, not translated from one another.
items.result: Posts go out every morning without me. 255 automated checks run before every release: if any of them fails, nothing gets published. It runs on my own home server.

items.title: Dumza — my own website monitoring SaaS
items.task: A service that checks websites, APIs and servers around the clock and alerts the owner the moment something goes down.
items.solution: Built solo — from architecture to billing and production. SSL certificate, domain and cron job monitoring, public status pages with incident history, Google sign-in and two-factor protection, subscriptions and an admin panel with an audit log. The architecture is ready for checks from different regions of the world.
items.result: Live at dumza.com: alerts via email, Telegram, Slack and webhooks, 8 languages, customers’ sensitive data is encrypted, and the code is covered by a hundred test files.

items.title: A trading bot for a crypto exchange
items.task: A learning project where I dug into automation: the system trades on Binance by itself using proven rules, and asks a human wherever judgement is needed.
items.solution: Two parts on one account: the bot trades by the rules on its own, while the radar spots opportunities and leaves the decision to me. Around them — tools for testing strategies and a server that updates itself.
items.result: On historical data the strategy was profitable in all 7 test quarters, even the worst one. The system currently runs on the exchange’s test account.

modules.title: Bot
modules.text: Trades its own list of coins. Waits for a deep 18% drawdown, buys in a ladder of 6 parts and sells each one separately at +3%. Before entering it waits for confirmation so it doesn’t react to random price spikes.

modules.title: Radar
modules.text: Watches a wider list of coins and messages me in Telegram when one drops sharply. It doesn’t buy on its own — I decide, with a button right in the chat. Balance, profit report and open positions are a command away there too. The radar has its own budget so it never touches the bot’s money.

modules.title: Alerts
modules.text: If a coin bought via the radar goes into the red, I get a message: when and at what price it was bought, what it’s worth now — and a “Close at market” button. I deliberately didn’t build an automatic stop-loss: the decision stays with a human.

modules.title: Signal journal
modules.text: The radar records every signal and later checks where the price went. That shows whether my manual picks help or whether taking every signal would have been better.

modules.title: Strategy testing
modules.text: Backtests on history, validation on data the strategy has never seen, a coin ranking and paper trading — before risking any money.

modules.title: Server and safety
modules.text: Runs 24/7 on a separate laptop: every 15 minutes it pulls updates, runs the tests, builds and restarts, rolling back on failure. Trades are stored in a database, so restarts break nothing. Real money only with an explicit flag on the server itself.

about.heading: Who builds your bot
paragraphs: I’ve been writing code for more than five years. I’ve built SaaS platforms, admin panels, trading interfaces for a crypto platform and websites for clients. In my last team I ran code reviews and sprint planning for six developers.
Right now I’m building Dumza on my own — my website monitoring service, from architecture to billing and production. And I build AI chatbots for businesses.
I know automation from practice: I’ve built my own AI chatbot engine for businesses, a trading bot for a crypto exchange and a system that runs a news channel by itself.

I don’t assemble bots in a drag-and-drop builder. I write each one for a specific business: your prices, your customers and the way you like to work. That’s why the bot sounds like you, not like an answering machine.
I work online — with clients from any country where there’s demand.

items.question: Who will build the bot?
items.answer: Me and my team. I lead the project from the first conversation to launch and edits and stay in touch with you myself, so you always know who’s responsible for the result. We don’t assemble bots in builders — every bot is written for your business.

items.question: How much does the bot cost per month after launch?
items.answer: Hosting and AI usage are paid separately, and it’s usually not much. I’ll give you the exact amount before we start: I run typical conversations for your business and calculate the usage. Bills go straight to you, with no markup from me.

items.question: What if the bot tells a customer something wrong?
items.answer: The bot only knows what you’ve told it about your business. If it doesn’t have the answer, it doesn’t make things up — it hands the chat to you. Unhappy customers and tricky questions also go straight to a human.

items.question: How long does the launch take?
items.answer: It depends on the task. A simple bot for one messenger usually takes up to two weeks, including testing.

items.question: Do I need any technical knowledge?
items.answer: No. I set everything up and launch it. From you I need prices, services and answers to common questions — in plain text.

items.question: Can I change prices or services later?
items.answer: Yes. Edits are free during the first two weeks; after that, by agreement or as part of VIP.
